newsitem.title: USA: GFOA urges SEC to revise investment adviser rule.
newsitem.headline: GFOA urges SEC to revise investment adviser rule.

text.p: GFOA urged the SEC to revise part of a proposed rule that tells investment advisers whether their activities fall under state or federal regulation.

The Government Finance Officers Associations outlined concerns in a seven-page comment letter to the Securities and Exchange Commission, which proposed rules last year to implement the Investment Advisers Supervision Coordination Act of 1996.
The act is actually Title III of a broad securities regulation reform law enacted last year by Congress called the National Securities Markets Improvement Act of 1996.
The new law authorizes the SEC to regulate advisers with over $25 million in assets under management. States are to regulate advisers with less than $25 million in assets.

The law defines assets under management as securities portfolios over which advisers have "continuous and regular supervisory or management services." But it lets SEC define what constitutes a securities portfolio.

SEC defines a securities portfiolio as one in which at least 50 percent of the total value of the account, less than cash, consists of securities. It excludes real estate, commodities and collectibles.

GFOA notes that the adviser must include the entire value of each portfolio, adding back in amounts for cash and non-securities positions. And, finally, the adviser must determine if it provides "continuous and regular supervisory or management services," GFOA said.

Such a three-part test is too "complicated," GFOA warned. "Under this formula, it would be possible for a portfolio to contain more than 50 percent in nonsecurities assets, because of the reduction for cash and cash equivalents, and still be considered a securities portfolio," GFOA said.
GFOA said it was not Congress' intent to designate assets under management as securities portfolios, and "believes that the portfolios should in fact be predominantly securities."

The group said a "substantially higher threshold should be set if cash and cash equivalents are to be included." Also, the $25 million threshold for securities portfolios should exclude real estate, commodities and collectibles, GFOA said.
